title: Prudence
hookLine: practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time

cards: "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going." That's Proverbs, and it could be pinned above every inbox. A text arrives: your package is on hold, tap here and pay a small fee.
One person taps before finishing the sentence. Another reads it twice, checks where it came from, and waits. Neither is necessarily smarter.
One just looked well to his going. Faith, hope and love were the virtues aimed at God. Now come the four that Christian teachers call the cardinal virtues, the ones for running an ordinary life.

teach.b: The four are named together in the Book of Wisdom, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and King James printings place among the Apocrypha.
Speaking of wisdom, it says: "for she teacheth temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude." Christian teachers took that list and built on it.

Prudence comes first in their order, because it steers the others. It's practical wisdom: knowing the right thing, the right way to do it, and the right time. Not cleverness, and not caution for its own sake.
A prudent person can be bold.

teach.h: WISE AS SERPENTS, HARMLESS AS DOVES.
teach.b: Jesus sends his disciples out with a strange pairing: "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." Sharp-eyed and gentle at once. That's prudence.
Ecclesiastes gives the timing part: there is "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." The same true words can heal at one moment and wound at another. Prudence notices which moment it is.

teach.h: A WEEK THAT NEEDED HOW AND WHEN.
teach.b: And this closes a week, so look back at what it's steered. Do not steal: give it back. A truthful witness: speak truly.
Do not covet: enough is enough. Then faith, trust. Hope, an anchor.
Love, the one that lasts. Each needs prudence to land well: knowing when to speak a hard truth, how to give something back without a scene, where a concrete act of love will actually help.
The commandments and the virtues say what. Prudence asks how, and when.

how: Catholic and Orthodox teaching names prudence among the cardinal virtues; some Christians practice it by praying before decisions, seeking counsel and weighing the timing of what they say and do.

games.q: a text says your package is on hold until you tap a link and pay a small fee. what does Proverbs' prudent person do?
o: tap it right away; the fee is small.
look well to your own steps: check where it came from, and wait.
forward it to friends to ask if it's real.
games.why: "the simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going."

practice: Bring to mind one choice waiting for you, a reply, a purchase, a conversation, and ask three plain questions: what is the right thing here, what's the right way to do it, and is now the right time?
Let each question sit for a few breaths without forcing an answer. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom, as the letter of James invites.

wordCard.voice: Prudence. Practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time. The virtue Christian teachers place first, to steer the rest.

orig.note: Greek: practical wisdom, good judgment; the word for prudence in Wisdom 8:7.

carryVoice: Your line: wise in the moment. Prudent can still mean bold. That's today, done.
